title: The Year of Release: Open Your Hand to the Poor
summary: Every seventh year Israelite creditors must release their fellow Israelites from debt. Moses warns against refusing loans as the year of release draws near and commands open-handed generosity to the poor. A Hebrew servant must be set free after six years and sent off with generous provisions, unless he chooses to stay for life. The chapter closes with the firstborn of the herds and flocks, which belong to God and are eaten at the sanctuary.
story: The law code that began in chapter 12 has moved from worship at the chosen place (chapter 12), through loyalty (chapter 13), to holiness at the table and the tithe for the poor (chapter 14). Chapter 15 builds on that last theme with the most radical economic laws in the Old Testament. The rhythm of seven that shaped the week now shapes the years: as the Sabbath gave rest to workers, the seventh year gives release to debtors and servants. The chapter rests the whole arrangement on Israel's own story, “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (verse 15). A people freed from slavery must not create a permanent underclass of their own.
historical:
Debt was the main road into poverty and servitude in the ancient Near East. A farmer hit by a poor harvest might borrow seed or food, and if he could not repay he might sell his land, then his children, and finally himself into servitude. Mesopotamian kings sometimes issued decrees, known in Akkadian as misharum (justice), canceling certain debts and freeing debt slaves; one of the best preserved is the edict of the Babylonian king Ammisaduqa in the seventeenth century BC. Those decrees depended on a king's decision. Deuteronomy makes release a fixed and regular part of the calendar, owed to every Israelite by law.

The Old Testament records both the ideal and its failure. Jeremiah 34 tells how the people of Jerusalem, under King Zedekiah during the Babylonian siege, freed their Hebrew slaves and then took them back, which Jeremiah condemns as a breach of this law. After the exile the community in Nehemiah 10:31 pledged to forgo the collection of debts in the seventh year. Around the turn of the era, according to Jewish tradition, the sage Hillel introduced a legal device called the prosbul, which allowed loans to be collected through the court so that people would not refuse to lend as the seventh year approached, the very problem verse 9 foresees.
cultural:
Verse 3 allows debts owed by a foreigner, meaning a trader or visitor rather than a resident sojourner, to be collected; the release protects members of the covenant community from being ground down by one another. The law for a Hebrew servant (verses 12 to 18) is also found in Exodus 21:2-6, but Deuteronomy adds two things: it applies explicitly to women as well as men, and it requires the master to send the freed servant off with a generous share of flock, grain, and wine, enough to start again. A servant who chose to remain was marked by having his ear pierced against the door of the house, a public sign that he now belonged permanently to that household.

The firstborn of the herds and flocks (verses 19 to 23) belonged to God, a principle rooted in the exodus, when God spared Israel's firstborn (Exodus 13). They could not be worked or sheared for profit, and they were eaten by the family at the sanctuary. A blemished animal could not be offered but could be eaten at home, under the same rule about blood as in chapter 12.
literary: The chapter is organized around the idea of release, with the key word shemittah and the verbs of letting go running through verses 1 to 18. It combines law with persuasion. Verses 4 to 6 state an ideal, that there will be no poor among you if Israel obeys, while verses 7 to 11 address the reality that there will be poor people, ending with the blunt admission of verse 11. The hand appears repeatedly: shut or open, the hand that lends, the hand God blesses. The chapter also speaks to motives, warning against a wicked thought in the heart (verse 9) and a grieving heart in giving (verse 10). Verses 19 to 23 on the firstborn form a short separate unit linked to the sanctuary laws of chapters 12 and 14.

Freeing Hebrew servants in the seventh year

doctrines.note: The law reaches into economics and debt, not only worship. It builds mercy into the structure of society so that poverty cannot become permanent, and it asks for a generous heart, not only outward compliance.
Israel's treatment of servants is grounded in their own redemption: God freed them from slavery, so they must free others. Grace received becomes the pattern for grace given.
Moses promises that the LORD will bless those who give generously. Israel's security in the land does not come from hoarding but from trusting God to provide.

words.note: Shemittah, release or remission. From a verb meaning to let drop or let go, it names the seventh-year canceling of debts. Interpreters differ on whether the debts were forgiven entirely or only suspended for that year; Jewish tradition took it as full cancellation. The word is still used in Judaism for the sabbatical year.

Evyon, needy or poor. It describes someone who lacks the basic means of life and is vulnerable to exploitation. The word appears six times in this chapter. Throughout the Psalms and Prophets, God is the defender of the evyon, and those who oppress them answer to him.

Patach, to open. Moses commands Israel to open their hand to the poor (verses 8 and 11), in contrast to shutting the hand and hardening the heart (verse 7). The image is concrete: generosity is a gesture of the body as well as the will.
Chophshi, free. It describes a servant released from service (verses 12, 13, and 18). The law did not abolish servitude, but it limited it and required that freedom come with the means to live.

christ: When Jesus announced his ministry in the synagogue at Nazareth, he read from Isaiah 61, which proclaims liberty to captives and the year of the LORD's favor (Luke 4:18-19), language that draws on the release laws of Deuteronomy and Leviticus. When he said, “The poor you will always have with you” (Matthew 26:11), he echoed verse 11, which is itself a command to keep giving, not an excuse to stop. The early church in Jerusalem shared its goods so that there was no needy person among them (Acts 4:34), which many readers see as fulfilling the ideal of verse 4. Christians have also read the release of debts as a picture of forgiveness in Christ. The Lord's Prayer asks God to forgive our debts as we forgive our debtors (Matthew 6:12), tying God's release of our sins to our release of others.

hard.q: Verse 4 says there will be no poor among you, but verse 11 says there will never cease to be poor. Is this a contradiction?
hard.a:
The two statements sit only a few verses apart, which suggests the writer saw them as belonging together. Most interpreters read verse 4 as a promise tied to a condition: there need be no poor among you if Israel obeys God's laws, including the laws of release and generosity (verse 5). Verse 11 speaks realistically about what will actually happen in a fallen world where people do not fully obey: there will always be poor people, and so the command to open the hand will always apply. Some see verse 4 as describing the goal the laws aim at and verse 11 as the ongoing situation they address.

The chapter also raises questions about servitude itself. The law permitted Israelites to be sold into service for debt, which modern readers find troubling. Interpreters note that the law limited this service to six years, required generous release, protected women equally, and grounded all of it in God's act of freeing Israel from slavery, which set a trajectory toward freedom. Christians differ on how far this trajectory should be traced in later history, but they agree that the chapter's heart is mercy toward the vulnerable.

questions: Verse 9 warns against a wicked thought that makes people stingy as the year of release approaches. What calculations tempt you to hold back from generosity?
Israel was to free servants because God had freed them. How does remembering what God has done for you change the way you treat people who owe you something?
The chapter holds together the ideal of no poor and the reality that the poor will always be present. How do you hold hope and realism together when you think about poverty?
